newsitem.title: UK: Fungus could counter river blindness, expert says.
newsitem.headline: Fungus could counter river blindness, expert says.

text.p: A fungus that hijacks egg production in buffalo gnats could offer a natural answer to river blindness, which afflicts millions in Africa and South America, a British expert said on Friday.

Stephen Moss of the University of Portsmouth said scientists were keenly studying a fungus that works as a natural birth-control agent in buffalo gnats, which carry a worm that blinds millions of people in west Africa and Venezuela.
Buffalo gnats or blackflies also proliferate in vast numbers in Canada and Scandinavia, sometimes sucking cattle literally dry and tormenting other victims.
Similar fungi infect mosquitoes and midges. Mosquitoes carry malaria, which infects million of people around the world, while midges multiply in vast numbers in places like Scotland.
The fungus, Harpella melusinae, normally infects the buffalo gnat with no symptoms at all. Sometimes, however, it invades the ovaries of the female fly and replaces its eggs with its own spore.

But the fly doesn't know this. "The fly still thinks it's got eggs," Moss told reporters at the British Association for the Advancement of Science's annual festival. So it still tries to lay eggs, instead laying spore and infecting more flies.

Moss said it would be decades before the fungus could be used commercially to fight the flies. His laboratory is studying how it reproduces and will then look to see if it could be genetically manipulated to cause more damage than it does already.
"It's in balance (now)," he said. "The whole idea, if you are going to control the organism, is to upset the balance."
He added: "If we can culture it, then we would release it into an area where the fly is."

But Moss warned that scientists would have to be careful. "You don't want to disrupt the entire ecology," he said. Fly larvae that live in water can help keep it clean and clear, while their droppings are food for other animals. Flies, of course, also feed bats and birds.

Fungi are already used to control pests like the Colorado potato beetle and aphids. Scientists genetically manipulate them to produce enzymes used in medicine, washing powders and food production -- a multi-billion dollar industry worldwide.
Moss said he knew of no reason the same techniques could not be used initially to make the fungus more effective against buffalo gnats, and then to alter it to attack mosquitoes, for instance.
